title: Uddalaka and the lump of clay
hookLine: a proud son comes home, and his father holds up clay
carry: one reality under every name and form
tomorrow: before anything existed: was there something, or nothing?

lines: A SON HOME, A LITTLE PROUD.
cards: Ads love this promise: learn one trick, and everything else falls into place. Usually it's a scam. In the Chandogya Upanishad, a father makes the same kind of promise to his son, and means it.
Shvetaketu has come home after years of study, sure of himself, a little full of himself. His father asks him one question.
Did you ask for the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, the unknown becomes known? It sounds impossible. How do you hear what you've never heard?

teach.b: Shvetaketu can't answer. How could there be such a teaching, sir? So the father, Uddalaka, reaches for the plainest thing in any village.
Clay. By one lump of clay, he says, everything made of clay is known.

teach.h: THE CHANGE IS ONLY A NAME.
teach.b: A pot, a cup, a lamp: the change is only a name, a matter of words. What's really there is clay. Then copper, and all that is made of copper.
Then iron, down to the nail-cutters. That solves the puzzle. Nobody needs to have seen every pot on earth to know what each one is made of.
Know the clay, and the unheard-of pot is already known. The father isn't promising trivia about everything.

He's pointing at the ground floor under everything. Vedanta teachers give it a name: name and form, nama-rupa, change; the one reality underneath, Brahman, doesn't. And Shvetaketu, to his credit, doesn't argue.
Surely my teachers didn't know this, he says, or why wouldn't they have told me?
Please, sir, teach me. That is the frame for the whole chapter. The saying this block is named for, tat tvam asi, that you are, hasn't been spoken yet.
When it comes, it will come from a father to a son, after a lesson on clay.

how: The sixth chapter of the Chandogya Upanishad, Uddalaka's teaching to his son Shvetaketu, is a standard text in Vedanta study, and a teacher may begin it with the clay example.

o: that belongs to you, so keep it close
that you are: you are that deeper reality
you should become like that, someday

games.q: the father, the son, the clay. tap the pairs.
p: the son home from study, a bit proud
the father who asks one question
by it, every clay thing is known
only a name, a matter of words

s: Shvetaketu came home without any learning
he had studied for years and was proud of it. what he hadn't asked for was the teaching underneath.
in the clay picture, the pot's name is only a matter of words
the change is only a name; what's really there is clay.
tat tvam asi is spoken at the very start of the chapter
it comes later. first, the father teaches with clay.

games.q: you're cramming vocabulary, and a friend says: learn the roots and you'll know words you've never seen. how would Uddalaka see that?
o: that's his move: know what's underneath, and the unseen is known.
impossible: you can only know what you've already studied.
a shortcut for lazy students, nothing like the clay.
games.why: know one lump of clay and every pot is known. the father teaches the ground floor under the names, not a longer list.

practice: Rest your eyes on one object near you: a cup, a bowl, a table. Let its name fall away for a moment, and notice only what it's made of. Breathe with that: the shape on top, the stuff underneath.

wordCard.voice: Tat tvam asi: that you are. In the Chandogya, a father will say it to his son, and he starts with a lump of clay.

orig.note: Sanskrit: that you are. tat (that) + tvam (you) + asi (are), from the Chandogya Upanishad.

carryVoice: Keep this one: one reality under every name and form, like one clay under many pots. Talk tomorrow.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.1.1–7 (Shvetaketu returns from study proud; his father asks whether he asked for the teaching by which the unheard is heard, the unthought thought, the unknown known; by one lump of clay all that is made of clay is known, the change being only a name, a matter of words, the reality being clay; likewise copper, and iron and nail-cutters; Shvetaketu: surely my teachers did not know this; please, sir, teach me)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7 (tat tvam asi, spoken later in the chapter)
